title: Hypoparathyroidism: Replace Calcium Safely, Control Phosphate, Protect the Kidneys
bottomLine: Hypoparathyroidism is hypocalcemia with an inappropriately low or normal PTH after magnesium and renal context are considered. Treat symptomatic severe hypocalcemia urgently, but long-term therapy must balance symptom control against hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis and renal injury.
recognize: Perioral or acral paresthesias, cramps, tetany, seizures and QT prolongation suggest clinically important hypocalcemia.
Postsurgical disease after thyroid/parathyroid surgery is common; autoimmune or genetic causes are considered when surgery does not explain it.
differentiate: Severe hypomagnesemia can suppress PTH secretion and create functional hypoparathyroidism.
Vitamin D deficiency, CKD and acute illness can also cause hypocalcemia but have different PTH/phosphate patterns.
assessment: Assess symptoms, ECG risk, recent neck surgery, calcium/vitamin D intake, magnesium, kidney disease, malabsorption and medications affecting calcium.
Review pregnancy status because calcium/calcitriol requirements and monitoring can change.
workup: Confirm calcium using albumin-adjusted or ionized calcium when appropriate and obtain PTH, phosphate, magnesium, creatinine/eGFR and 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
During chronic therapy, monitor serum calcium/phosphate/renal function and urinary calcium according to specialty guidance.
management: Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium while the cause and magnesium are corrected.

Chronic hypoparathyroidism is generally managed with oral calcium plus active vitamin D, individualized to maintain clinical stability while avoiding high-normal calcium targets that increase urinary calcium.
medicationSafety: Excess calcium/calcitriol can cause hypercalcemia and hypercalciuria even when symptoms improve.
Thiazide strategies for hypercalciuria require BP, sodium and potassium monitoring and are individualized.
redFlags: Acute kidney injury or recurrent stones during therapy
counselling: Teach symptoms of both low and high calcium and the importance of prescribed monitoring rather than self-escalating supplements.
followUp: Reassess after meaningful dose, pregnancy, renal-function or symptom changes and involve endocrinology when control is difficult.
examTrap: Chasing a high-normal serum calcium with progressively more calcium/calcitriol while ignoring rising urinary calcium and renal risk.
oneLinePearl: In hypoparathyroidism, enough calcium to prevent symptoms is the goal—not the highest normal calcium you can achieve.
sourceBasis: International Task Force hypoparathyroidism guidance used where Canadian-specific detail is not published

title: Vitamin D: Test Selectively, Treat Deficiency, Avoid Megadose Thinking
bottomLine: Do not order 25-hydroxyvitamin D as a universal wellness test. Test when deficiency risk or a bone/mineral disorder makes the result actionable, treat confirmed clinically important deficiency with an appropriate regimen, and avoid high-dose supplementation as a substitute for fracture-risk treatment.
recognize: Risk rises with malabsorption, CKD/liver disease, osteoporosis/fragility fracture, limited intake or sun exposure and selected medications.
Severe deficiency can contribute to osteomalacia, muscle weakness and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
differentiate: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the usual test of vitamin D status; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not a routine deficiency test.
Routine vitamin D supplementation in unselected adults is not equivalent to treating documented deficiency or supporting osteoporosis pharmacotherapy.
assessment: Clarify why testing would change management and assess calcium/phosphate disorders, fracture risk, malabsorption, kidney/liver disease and supplement use.
workup: Use 25-hydroxyvitamin D when testing is indicated; pair with calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH and renal testing when osteomalacia or another metabolic bone disorder is plausible.
management: Use an evidence-based replacement strategy appropriate to severity and cause, then transition to maintenance sufficient for the patient's clinical context.
Treat malabsorption or other causes and use osteoporosis-specific therapy when fracture risk warrants it rather than relying on vitamin D alone.
medicationSafety: Excess vitamin D can cause hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria and kidney injury.
Avoid repeated pharmacologic megadoses without a defined indication and monitoring plan.
counselling: Explain that more vitamin D is not automatically better and that routine testing is unnecessary for many healthy adults.
followUp: Repeat levels only when the result will change therapy, such as significant deficiency, malabsorption, unusual dosing needs or metabolic bone disease.
examTrap: Ordering vitamin D levels annually for every adult—or treating high fracture risk with vitamin D alone instead of fracture-risk pharmacotherapy.
oneLinePearl: Vitamin D is a targeted test and treatment—not a universal screening score.
sourceBasis: Osteoporosis Canada 2026 calcium/vitamin D evidence update
Choosing Wisely Canada Vitamin D Testing

title: Osteoporosis: Treat Fracture Risk, Not a T-Score in Isolation
bottomLine: Canadian osteoporosis treatment is fracture-risk based. A prior hip/vertebral or multiple fragility fractures, high FRAX risk or sufficiently low BMD in the appropriate age/risk context can justify pharmacotherapy; bisphosphonates are first-line for most people starting treatment.
recognize: Fragility fracture is a major risk signal even when BMD is not dramatically low.
Recent fracture carries especially high near-term risk and should trigger secondary-fracture prevention.
differentiate: Osteopenic BMD is not synonymous with low fracture risk; FRAX and clinical risk factors matter.
Osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, myeloma and other secondary bone diseases require cause-specific care.
assessment: Assess prior fractures, falls, parental hip fracture, glucocorticoids, smoking, alcohol, weight loss, secondary causes, renal function, dental/swallowing issues and treatment preferences.
workup: Use BMD and Canada-specific FRAX when indicated; evaluate calcium, phosphate, creatinine, ALP, TSH and selected secondary causes according to clinical risk.
Use vertebral imaging when history/height loss/BMD risk suggests occult vertebral fracture.
management: Offer alendronate, risedronate or zoledronic acid first-line for most eligible patients, individualized for renal/GI/access factors.
Denosumab can be used when appropriate but requires a planned antiresorptive transition if stopped; high/very-high risk disease may need specialist anabolic/sequence strategies.
medicationSafety: Review renal function and oral bisphosphonate administration contraindications.
New thigh/groin pain raises atypical femoral fracture concern; jaw symptoms/dental context matter for osteonecrosis risk.
Do not stop denosumab without a follow-on antiresorptive plan because rebound vertebral fractures can occur.
redFlags: Multiple vertebral fractures or very-high-risk disease
counselling: Discuss exercise, falls prevention, adequate calcium/vitamin D and medication duration as part of fracture prevention—not as substitutes for indicated therapy.
followUp: Monitor adherence, interval fractures, adverse effects and BMD/risk at guideline-appropriate intervals rather than repeating DXA too frequently.
examTrap: Withholding treatment after a fragility hip fracture because the T-score is only osteopenic—or stopping denosumab without transition therapy.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis treatment prevents fractures; the T-score is only one part of the risk story.
sourceBasis: Osteoporosis Canada 2026 calcium/vitamin D evidence update

title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Build the Calcium–Phosphate–PTH Pattern
bottomLine: When bone pain, fractures or abnormal calcium/phosphate/ALP suggest metabolic bone disease, define the mineral pattern before naming osteoporosis. Calcium, phosphate, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, renal function and ALP often reveal whether the problem is deficiency, parathyroid disease, CKD-mineral bone disorder or another process.
recognize: Bone pain, proximal weakness, fractures, growth/deformity findings or unexplained ALP/mineral abnormalities can signal osteomalacia/rickets or another metabolic bone disorder.
CKD changes phosphate, PTH and vitamin D physiology and should not be treated as routine primary osteoporosis.
differentiate: Osteoporosis is reduced bone strength without a mineralization defect; osteomalacia/rickets reflect impaired mineralization.
Paget disease can cause focal high bone turnover/ALP with characteristic imaging and requires a different evaluation.
assessment: Assess diet, malabsorption, bariatric surgery, kidney/liver disease, medications, fractures, pain, weakness, growth history and family/genetic clues.
workup: Use calcium, phosphate, ALP, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and renal function as the core pattern; add urine studies, celiac testing, protein electrophoresis, imaging or genetic/specialty tests when the phenotype supports them.
management: Treat the identified cause and correct clinically important mineral abnormalities; refer complex CKD-MBD, unexplained fractures, severe mineralization disease or rare bone disease.
medicationSafety: Antiresorptives can be inappropriate before severe hypocalcemia/osteomalacia is corrected.
Renal impairment materially changes several bone-drug choices.
redFlags: Advanced CKD with major mineral abnormalities
counselling: Explain that 'weak bones' can arise from different mechanisms and the laboratory pattern determines the treatment.
followUp: Trend the abnormal mineral axis after treatment and confirm clinical/biochemical response rather than relying on symptoms alone.
examTrap: Calling every low-BMD or fracture presentation osteoporosis before checking for osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism or CKD-mineral bone disease.
oneLinePearl: Metabolic bone diagnosis starts with the mineral pattern, not the DXA label.

title: Pituitary Adenoma: Hormone Excess, Hormone Loss, or Mass Effect?
bottomLine: A pituitary lesion is managed by three questions: is it secreting hormone, is it causing pituitary failure, and is it compressing the optic apparatus or other structures? Sudden severe headache with visual/neurologic decline is pituitary apoplexy until excluded.
recognize: Prolactin excess, acromegalic features, Cushing phenotype, menstrual/sexual dysfunction, hypothyroid/adrenal symptoms or bitemporal visual loss can reveal a pituitary tumour.
Incidental microlesions without hormonal or compressive effects are different from macroadenomas with mass effect.
differentiate: Medication-induced hyperprolactinemia and stalk effect differ from a prolactinoma; very large tumours can create assay hook-effect pitfalls.
Central hypothyroidism has low free T4 with an inappropriately low/normal TSH.
assessment: Assess headache, visual symptoms, galactorrhea, menstrual/sexual function, growth/acromegalic change, cortisol symptoms, polyuria/polydipsia and pregnancy.
workup: Use prolactin, IGF-1, thyroid axis and cortisol-axis testing as indicated, plus pituitary MRI and formal visual fields when the lesion approaches/compresses the chiasm.
Interpret pituitary hormones as axes, not isolated 'normal range' numbers.
management: Prolactinomas are often treated medically with dopamine agonist therapy; compressive, non-prolactin secreting or other functional tumours may require transsphenoidal surgery/specialty therapy.
Pituitary hormone deficiencies require replacement with attention to adrenal status before thyroid replacement when both may be deficient.
medicationSafety: Starting levothyroxine in unrecognized cortisol deficiency can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Dopamine agonist monitoring and pregnancy plans require endocrine follow-up.
redFlags: Thunderclap/severe headache with visual loss or ophthalmoplegia
counselling: Explain that a pituitary adenoma can affect several hormone systems and follow-up depends on both size and function.
followUp: Coordinate endocrinology/neurosurgery/ophthalmology follow-up with hormone and imaging surveillance matched to tumour type.
examTrap: Treating low free T4 with levothyroxine before checking the cortisol axis in a patient with a pituitary mass.
oneLinePearl: Pituitary lesions are about secretion, deficiency and compression—check all three.
sourceBasis: Pituitary Society/Endocrine Society guidance where Canadian-specific guidance is not published

title: PCOS: Treat Reproductive and Metabolic Risk Together
bottomLine: PCOS is more than irregular periods. Confirm the syndrome after excluding important mimics, then address cycle/endometrial protection, hyperandrogenism or fertility goals and long-term metabolic risk using non-stigmatizing shared decision-making.
recognize: Ovulatory dysfunction, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology define the diagnostic framework; ultrasound is not mandatory when the other required features are established in an appropriate adult.
Insulin resistance, dysglycemia, sleep apnea, dyslipidemia and cardiovascular risk factors are common comorbidities.
differentiate: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumours can mimic PCOS.
Rapid virilization or markedly progressive androgen symptoms require evaluation beyond routine PCOS.
assessment: Assess menstrual pattern, hyperandrogen symptoms, fertility goals, pregnancy possibility, BP, adiposity-related complications, sleep, mental health/eating disorder symptoms and medications.
workup: Use pregnancy testing and targeted TSH/prolactin/androgen or other exclusion testing; screen glycemia and cardiovascular risk using current PCOS guidance.
Do not repeatedly image ovaries as a measure of treatment response.
management: Use combined hormonal contraception or another endometrial-protection strategy when pregnancy is not desired and cycles are infrequent, individualized for contraindications.
Metformin is useful particularly for metabolic/glycemic indications and selected cycle/fertility contexts; fertility treatment follows ovulation-induction guidance when pregnancy is desired.
Treat obesity/metabolic complications with the same evidence-based options offered to patients without PCOS when indicated.
medicationSafety: Review thrombotic/estrogen contraindications before combined hormonal contraception.
Antiandrogens require reliable pregnancy prevention because of fetal risk.
counselling: Avoid framing PCOS as a weight failure; discuss metabolic and reproductive goals separately and explicitly.
followUp: Track cycles/endometrial protection, metabolic risk, BP, symptoms and fertility goals rather than ovarian morphology.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS from an ultrasound alone—or focusing on weight while ignoring prolonged anovulation and endometrial protection.
oneLinePearl: PCOS care protects the endometrium today and metabolic health for the long term.

title: Lipid Disorders: Risk Stratification Before Intensification
bottomLine: Canadian lipid treatment is risk-based. Identify established ASCVD and statin-indicated conditions first, estimate primary-prevention risk when appropriate, then use maximally tolerated statin therapy and evidence-based nonstatin intensification according to residual risk and lipid thresholds.
recognize: Clinical ASCVD, abdominal aortic aneurysm, most diabetes/CKD and LDL-C at or above 5 mmol/L are high-value treatment contexts.
Very high LDL-C or premature ASCVD suggests familial hypercholesterolemia; severe triglyceride elevation can shift the immediate concern toward pancreatitis.
differentiate: Primary-prevention treatment is not based on LDL-C alone except in very-high LDL/FH situations.
When triglycerides are above 1.5 mmol/L, non-HDL-C or ApoB can be more informative than LDL-C for risk/treatment assessment.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, diabetes, CKD, BP, smoking, family history, pregnancy plans, medications, secondary causes, alcohol and treatment preference/access.
workup: Use a lipid profile and Canadian risk estimator when applicable; consider one-time Lp(a) measurement as part of lifetime risk assessment.
Target thyroid, renal, hepatic or other secondary-cause testing to the clinical pattern.
management: Use high-intensity or maximally tolerated statin therapy in secondary prevention and guideline-indicated primary prevention.

Add ezetimibe and/or PCSK9-directed therapy in appropriate high-risk patients whose LDL-C/non-HDL/ApoB remains above CCS intensification thresholds; selected patients with elevated triglycerides may qualify for prescription icosapent ethyl.
medicationSafety: Evaluate significant muscle symptoms, major interactions and hepatic injury clinically rather than ordering repetitive CK/liver tests in every asymptomatic patient.
Pregnancy/planning pregnancy requires medication-specific review of lipid-lowering therapy.
redFlags: Very high triglycerides with pancreatitis symptoms
Severe muscle weakness/dark urine on therapy
counselling: Explain absolute cardiovascular risk and expected benefit rather than labelling one cholesterol number as 'good' or 'bad'.
followUp: Recheck response/adherence after therapy changes and then at clinically useful intervals.
examTrap: Withholding statin therapy from a secondary-prevention patient because the baseline LDL-C is not dramatically elevated.
oneLinePearl: Treat vascular risk first; use the lipid numbers to choose and intensify the strategy.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society 2021 Dyslipidemia Guideline and current CCS tools

title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy: Match the Drug to Complications, Goals, and Long-Term Use
bottomLine: Obesity pharmacotherapy is chronic-disease treatment, not a short cosmetic course. Assess adiposity-related complications, goals, contraindications, pregnancy, cost/access and patient preference, then select a Health Canada-approved long-term therapy and monitor health outcomes as well as weight.
recognize: Obesity Canada 2025 guidance supports pharmacotherapy for appropriate adults with BMI/adiposity thresholds and complications, individualized beyond BMI alone.
Semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, naltrexone/bupropion and orlistat have different efficacy, adverse-effect and comorbidity profiles.
differentiate: A drug approved for diabetes at one dose is not automatically equivalent to the obesity indication/dose.
Compounded or unapproved weight-loss products should not be substituted for approved therapies simply because access is difficult.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight; assess diabetes, ASCVD/HF, OSA, liver disease, eating disorder symptoms, mental health, gallbladder/pancreatic history, seizure/opioid use, GI disease, pregnancy plans, cost/coverage and prior treatment response.
workup: Use cause/complication-directed assessment rather than routine endocrine panels for every patient; establish baseline outcomes that the chosen drug can improve or worsen.
management: Offer pharmacotherapy with health-behaviour support when guideline criteria and patient goals support it.
Continue effective therapy long term when benefits outweigh harms because stopping often leads to weight regain and loss of health benefit; change therapy when response/tolerability is inadequate.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy is a key contraindication/stop context for weight-loss pharmacotherapy; ensure product-specific preconception timing.

Naltrexone/bupropion is inappropriate with uncontrolled seizure risk or active opioid therapy; GLP-1/GIP-based therapies require GI/gallbladder/pancreatic risk assessment and peri-procedural planning.
redFlags: Suicidal/major psychiatric deterioration where medication may contribute
counselling: Use person-first, non-stigmatizing language and define success by health, function and patient goals—not only kilograms lost.
followUp: Track adverse effects, cardiometabolic outcomes, function, adherence/access and weight trajectory; reassess continuation using product/guideline evidence rather than an arbitrary short trial.
examTrap: Treating obesity medication as a three-month kick-start and stopping an effective therapy without a maintenance plan.
oneLinePearl: Obesity medication works like other chronic-disease therapy: match it well, monitor it, and continue it when it is helping.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada Adult Clinical Practice Guideline — Pharmacotherapy updated 2025

title: Sodium and Potassium Disorders: Neurologic Tonicity vs Cardiac Electricity
bottomLine: Sodium disorders are interpreted through tonicity, chronicity, volume status and neurologic symptoms; potassium disorders are interpreted through severity, ECG/arrhythmia risk, renal function and ongoing shifts/losses. Treat dangerous physiology first while correcting the cause at a safe rate.
recognize: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia can cause seizure/encephalopathy; overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination.
Hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening conduction disturbance even before dramatic symptoms; hypokalemia increases arrhythmia risk, especially with magnesium deficiency or digoxin.
differentiate: Confirm hypotonic hyponatremia before applying SIADH reasoning; hyperglycemia and other osmoles can lower measured sodium without true hypotonicity.
Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis must be considered in a stable patient with an unexpected result, but a dangerous ECG/presentation is treated immediately.
assessment: Assess mental status/seizure, volume status, intake/output, GI losses, kidney/adrenal disease, medications and glucose for sodium disorders.
For potassium, assess ECG symptoms/rhythm, renal function, acid-base status, insulin/beta-agonist shifts, GI loss and RAAS-blocking/potassium-raising drugs.
workup: Use serum osmolality, glucose and urine osmolality/sodium selectively for hyponatremia classification.
Repeat potassium when pseudohyperkalemia is plausible and safe, but obtain ECG and urgent chemistry when severe true hyperkalemia is possible.
management: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia requires monitored hypertonic-saline therapy using a protocol with correction limits and frequent sodium checks.
Dangerous hyperkalemia management has three separate jobs: stabilize myocardium with IV calcium when indicated, shift potassium intracellularly, and remove potassium while correcting the cause.
Replace potassium and magnesium safely in clinically important hypokalemia.
medicationSafety: Thiazides, SSRIs and other drugs can contribute to hyponatremia; ACEi/ARB/MRA and potassium supplements can contribute to hyperkalemia.
Do not use a fixed sodium-correction target without considering chronicity and osmotic-demyelination risk.
redFlags: Severe potassium abnormality with renal failure
counselling: Review sick-day/medication and fluid advice only after the electrolyte mechanism is known; generic 'drink more water' can worsen hyponatremia.
followUp: Recheck electrolytes at a cadence matched to severity and after medication/cause correction; recurrent disorders need etiologic workup.
examTrap: Giving free water advice to unexplained hyponatremia—or treating hyperkalemia only with a shifting agent without addressing cardiac stabilization and potassium removal.
oneLinePearl: Sodium threatens the brain; potassium threatens the rhythm—classify the mechanism while treating the danger.

title: Calcium Disorders: Confirm the Calcium, Then Let PTH Split the Differential
bottomLine: Confirm a true calcium abnormality using albumin context or ionized calcium when needed, then use PTH to divide hypercalcemia into PTH-dependent versus PTH-independent causes. Severe symptomatic calcium disturbance is an acute-care problem; chronic treatment depends on the cause.
recognize: Hypercalcemia can cause dehydration/polyuria, constipation, weakness, confusion and shortened QT; severe cases can cause arrhythmia or kidney injury.
Hypocalcemia can cause paresthesias, cramps/tetany, seizure and prolonged QT.
differentiate: High/inappropriately normal PTH in hypercalcemia suggests primary/tertiary hyperparathyroid physiology; suppressed PTH redirects toward malignancy, vitamin D, medications and other causes.
Hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism differs from vitamin D deficiency, CKD and severe hypomagnesemia by its PTH/phosphate pattern.
assessment: Assess symptoms, volume status, kidney stones, fractures/bone pain, malignancy clues, medications/supplements, immobilization, kidney disease, neck surgery and magnesium status.
workup: Repeat/confirm calcium and obtain PTH, creatinine/eGFR, phosphate and magnesium; add 25-hydroxyvitamin D, PTHrP, electrophoresis or imaging only when the mechanism supports it.
Do not order parathyroid imaging to diagnose primary hyperparathyroidism; imaging is for operative localization after biochemical diagnosis.
management: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires IV volume resuscitation and cause/severity-directed acute therapy; malignancy-associated disease often needs antiresorptive treatment and oncology care.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium and magnesium correction; chronic therapy is cause-specific.
medicationSafety: Thiazides, lithium, calcium/vitamin D supplements and selected cancer therapies can alter calcium.
Antiresorptives can worsen hypocalcemia if vitamin D/calcium status and renal context are not addressed.
counselling: Advise against self-escalating calcium/vitamin D while the cause is unknown and explain why PTH changes the diagnostic pathway.
followUp: Trend calcium/renal function after treatment and close the loop on parathyroid, malignancy or metabolic-bone referral when indicated.
examTrap: Ordering a sestamibi scan to 'diagnose' primary hyperparathyroidism before establishing biochemical PTH-dependent hypercalcemia.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the calcium; then PTH tells you which half of the hypercalcemia differential to enter.
